Microwave ovens pose no problems to pacemaker function, but the affected arm should not be raised above the shoulder until approved by the cardiologist. The pacing current of an implanted pacemaker is not felt by the patient, but an external transcutaneous pacemaker may cause uncomfortable chest muscle contractions.

questions.question: A patient on the telemetry unit goes into VF and is unresponsive. Following initiation of the emergency call system (Code Blue), what would the nurse do next?

choices.text: Begin CPR.
Get the crash cart.
Administer amiodarone IV.
Defibrillate with 360 joules.

questions.rationale: Until the defibrillator is available, the patient needs CPR. Defibrillation is needed as soon as possible, so someone should bring the crash cart to the room. Amiodarone is an antidysrhythmic that is part of the advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) protocol for ventricular fibrillation. Defibrillation would be with 360 joules for monophasic defibrillators and 120 to 200 joules for biphasic defibrillators.

questions.question: The use of radiofrequency catheter ablation therapy to "burn" areas of the cardiac conduction system is indicated for the treatment of which problem?

choices.text: Sinus arrest
Heart blocks
Tachydysrhythmias
Premature ventricular beats

questions.rationale: Catheter ablation therapy uses radiofrequency energy to ablate or "burn" accessory pathways or ectopic sites in the atria, AV node, or ventricles that cause tachydysrhythmias. It is not used for sinus arrest, heart blocks, or premature ventricular beats.

questions.question: A patient with chest pain that is unrelieved by nitroglycerin is admitted to the coronary care unit for observation and diagnosis. While the patient has continuous ECG monitoring, what finding would most concern the nurse?

choices.text: Occasional PVCs
QRS complex change
ST segment elevation
A PR interval of 0.18 second

questions.rationale: ST segment elevation indicates injury or infarction of an area of the heart. A widened QRS occurs with second-degree AV block, type II and antidysrhythmic drugs. Occasional PVCs may be normal or may be the result of electrolyte imbalance or hypoxia. They require continued observation. A PR interval of 0.18 second is within normal range.

questions.question: A 54-year-old patient who has no structural heart disease has an episode of syncope. A head-up tilt-test is performed to rule out cardioneurogenic syncope. What will the patient experience if cardioneurogenic syncope is the problem?

choices.text: No change in HR or BP
Palpitations and dizziness
Tachydysrhythmias and chest pain
Marked bradycardia and hypotension

questions.rationale: One of the most common causes of syncope is cardioneurogenic syncope, or "vasovagal" syncope. In this type of syncope, there is accentuated adrenergic activity in the upright position, with intense activation of cardiopulmonary receptors resulting in marked bradycardia and hypotension, cerebral hypoperfusion, and syncope. Normally testing with the head-up tilt-test causes activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and compensation to increase CO and maintain BP when blood pools in the extremities.

questions.question: The patient is brought to the emergency department with acute coronary syndrome (ACS). What changes would the nurse expect to see on the ECG if only myocardial injury has occurred?

choices.text: Absent P wave
A wide QT interval
Tall, peaked T wave
ST-segment elevation

questions.rationale: ST segment elevation is seen in myocardial injury. An absent or buried P wave can occur with PVCs, ventricular tachycardia, or ventricular fibrillation. A wide pathologic QT interval affects repolarization and is caused by drugs and electrolyte imbalances. Tall, peaked T waves may be seen with electrolyte imbalance.

questions.question: Identify each cardiac rhythm using the systematic approach to assessing cardiac rhythms. All rhythm strips are 6 seconds.

options.text: Normal sinus rhythm with a run of PSVT

questions.rationale: a. Third-degree AV block: atrial and ventricular dissociation with regular atrial rate. b. Atrial flutter: saw-toothed flutter waves from the same ectopic foci. c. PVC, unifocal bigeminy: early occurrence of a wide, distorted QRS complex every other beat. d. Sinus bradycardia with ST depression: rate < 60 bpm. e. Second-degree AV block, type I: progressively lengthening PR interval until a QRS complex is blocked; left bundle branch block. f. PAC: irregular rate and rhythm and different P wave shape. g. Second-degree AV block, type II: regular atrial rate and PR interval, ventricular rate irregular with blocked QRS complexes. h. Sinus tachycardia: rate > 100 bpm but < 180 bpm. i. First-degree AV block: PR interval > 0.20; QRS > 0.12 which indicates a bundle branch block. j. Ventricular fibrillation: irregular chaotic waveforms of varying shapes and amplitude. k. PVC, unifocal trigeminy: early occurrence of a wide, distorted QRS complex every third beat. l. Atrial fibrillation, controlled ventricular response: accelerated atrial rate with chaotic fibrillatory waves and irregular ventricular rate; HR < 101 bpm. m. Normal sinus rhythm with a run of PSVT: atrial and ventricular rate increases to 375 bpm briefly before normal conduction resumes; could be caused by an atrial dysrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation or flutter. n. Normal sinus rhythm: starts at the SA node with rate of 60 to 100 bpm and follows the normal conduction pathway. o. Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia: rate of 150 to 250 bpm with wide distorted QRS complex.

questions.question: A 20-year-old patient has acute infective endocarditis. What topics would the nurse ask the patient about during the health history? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Renal dialysis
IV drug use
Recent dental work
Cardiac catheterization
Recent urinary tract infection

questions.rationale: Recent dental, urologic, surgical, or gynecologic procedures and history of IV drug abuse, heart disease, cardiac catheterization or surgery, renal dialysis, and infections all increase the risk of infective endocarditis.

questions.question: A patient has an admitting diagnosis of acute left-sided infective endocarditis. What is the best test to confirm this diagnosis?

choices.text: Three blood cultures
Complete blood count
Cardiac catheterization
Transesophageal echocardiogram

questions.rationale: Three positive blood cultures drawn over a 1-hour period from 3 different sites are the primary diagnostic tool for infective endocarditis. Although a complete blood count (CBC) will reveal a mild leukocytosis, this is a nonspecific finding. Cardiac catheterization is used when surgical intervention is being considered. Transesophageal echocardiograms can identify vegetations on valves but are used when blood cultures are negative.

questions.question: Which manifestation of infective endocarditis is a result of fragmentation and microembolization of vegetative lesions?

choices.text: Petechiae
Roth's spots
Osler's nodes
Splinter hemorrhages

questions.rationale: Petechiae from fragmentation and microembolization of vegetative lesions are seen as small hemorrhages in the conjunctiva, lips, and buccal mucosa and over the ankles, feet, and antecubital and popliteal areas. Roth's spots are hemorrhagic retinal lesions seen with funduscopic examination. Osler's nodes are lesions on the fingertips or toes. The cause of Roth's spots and Osler's nodes is not clear. Splinter hemorrhages are black longitudinal streaks that occur on nail beds. They may be caused by vessel damage from vasculitis or microemboli.

questions.question: Which statement describes Janeway's lesions as manifestations of infective endocarditis?

choices.text: Hemorrhagic retinal lesions
Black longitudinal streaks in nail beds
Painful red or purple lesions on fingers or toes
Flat, red, painless spots on the palm of hands and soles of feet

questions.rationale: Janeway's lesions are flat, painless, small red spots found on the fingertips, palms of hands, the soles of feet, and toes. Hemorrhagic retinal lesions are Roth's spots. Black streaks on the nails are splinter hemorrhages. Painful lesions on the fingertips and toes are Osler's nodes.

questions.question: A patient with infective endocarditis of a prosthetic mitral valve develops left hemiparesis and vision changes. What would the nurse expect to be included in interprofessional care?

choices.text: Embolectomy
Surgical valve replacement
Administration of anticoagulants
Higher-than-usual antibiotic dosages

questions.rationale: Early valve replacement followed by prolonged antibiotic and anticoagulant therapy is recommended for these patients. Drug therapy for patients who develop endocarditis of prosthetic valves is often unsuccessful in eliminating the infection and preventing embolization.

questions.question: A patient with aortic valve endocarditis develops dyspnea, crackles in the lungs, and restlessness. What complication would the nurse suspect?

choices.text: Pulmonary embolization from valve vegetations
Vegetative embolization to the coronary arteries
Valvular incompetence with resulting heart failure
Nonspecific manifestations that accompany infectious diseases

questions.rationale: The dyspnea, crackles, and restlessness that the patient is manifesting are manifestations of heart failure and decreased cardiac output (CO) that occurs in up to 80% of patients with aortic valve endocarditis because of aortic valve incompetence. Pulmonary emboli occur in right-sided endocarditis. Vegetative embolization from the aortic valve occurs throughout the arterial system and may affect any body organ.

questions.question: A patient hospitalized for 1 week with subacute infective endocarditis is afebrile and has no signs of heart damage. Discharge with outpatient antibiotic therapy is planned. During discharge planning with the patient, what is it most important for the nurse to do?

choices.text: Plan how his needs will be met while he continues on bed rest.
Encourage the use of diversional activities to relieve boredom and restlessness.
Teach the patient to avoid crowds and exposure to upper respiratory infections.
Assess the patient's home environment in terms of family assistance and hospital access.

questions.rationale: The patient with outpatient antibiotic therapy needs vigilant home nursing care. It is most important to determine the adequacy of the home environment for successful management of the patient. The patient is at risk for life-threatening complications, such as embolization and pulmonary edema, and must be able to access a hospital if needed. Bed rest will not be necessary for the patient without heart damage. Avoiding infections and planning diversional activities are indicated for the patient but are not the most important factors while he is on outpatient antibiotic therapy.

questions.question: What would the nurse teach the patient who has had endocarditis about preventing recurrence of the infection?

choices.text: Start on antibiotic therapy when exposed to persons with infections.
Take one aspirin a day to prevent vegetative lesions from forming around the valves.
Always maintain continuous antibiotic therapy to prevent the development of any systemic infection.
Obtain prophylactic antibiotic therapy before certain invasive medical or dental procedures (e.g., dental cleaning).

questions.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotic therapy should be started before invasive dental, medical, or surgical procedures to prevent recurrence of endocarditis. Symptoms of infection should be treated promptly, but antibiotics are not used for exposure to infection. Continuous antibiotic therapy is indicated only in patients with implanted devices or ongoing invasive procedure.

questions.question: A patient is admitted to the hospital with a suspected acute pericarditis. What is the best method for the nurse to use when assessing for the presence of a pericardial friction rub?

choices.text: Timing the sounds with the respiratory pattern
Place the bell of the stethoscope at the apical area of the heart
Use the diaphragm of the stethoscope to auscultate for a high-pitched continuous rumbling sound
Place the stethoscope at the lower left sternal border, patient leaning forward and holding breath

questions.rationale: The stethoscope diaphragm at the lower left sternal border with the patient leaning forward is the best method to use to hear the high-pitched, grating sound of a pericardial friction rub. The sound does not radiate widely and occurs with the heartbeat. To differentiate a pericardial friction rub from a pleural friction rub, have the patient hold their breath. The rub will still be heard if it is cardiac in nature.

questions.question: A patient with acute pericarditis has markedly distended jugular veins, decreased BP, tachycardia, tachypnea, and muffled heart sounds. What does the nurse recognize as the cause of these manifestations?

choices.text: The pericardial space is obliterated with scar tissue and thickened pericardium.
Excess pericardial fluid compresses the heart and prevents adequate diastolic filling.
The parietal and visceral pericardial membranes adhere to each other, preventing normal myocardial contraction
Fibrin accumulation on the visceral pericardium infiltrates the myocardium, creating myocardial dysfunction.

questions.rationale: The patient is experiencing cardiac tamponade that consists of excess fluid in the pericardial sac, which compresses the heart and the adjoining structures, preventing normal filling and cardiac output. A scarred and thickened pericardium, adherent pericardial membranes, and fibrin accumulation occur in chronic constrictive pericarditis.

questions.question: Which statements explain the measurement of pulsus paradoxus with cardiac tamponade? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A difference of < 10 mm Hg occurs.
A difference of > 10 mm Hg occurs.
It is measured with an automatic sphygmomanometer.
Rapidly inflate the cuff until you hear sounds throughout the respiratory cycle.
Subtract the number when sounds are heard in the respiratory cycle from the number when the first Korotkoff sound during expiration is heard.

questions.rationale: Pulsus paradoxus is measured with a manually operated sphygmomanometer. The cuff is deflated slowly until the first Korotkoff sound during expiration is heard and the number is noted. The slow deflation of the cuff is continued until sounds are heard throughout the respiratory cycle and that number is subtracted from the first number. When the difference is > 10 mm Hg, cardiac tamponade may be present. The difference is normally < 10 mm Hg.

questions.question: The patient with acute pericarditis is having a pericardiocentesis. What complication would the nurse monitor the patient for after surgery?

choices.text: Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
Myocardial infarction (MI)
Cerebrovascular accident (CVA)

questions.rationale: Pneumothorax may occur as a needle is inserted into the pericardial space to remove fluid for analysis and relieve cardiac pressure with pericardiocentesis. Other complications could include dysrhythmias, further cardiac tamponade, pneumomediastinum, myocardial laceration, and coronary artery laceration. Pneumonia, MI, and CVA would not be expected.

questions.question: A patient with acute pericarditis has pain from pericardial inflammation. What is the best nursing intervention for the patient?

choices.text: Administer opioids as prescribed on a round-the-clock schedule.
Promote progressive relaxation exercises with the use of deep, slow breathing.
Position the patient on the right side with the head of the bed elevated 15 degrees.
Position the patient in Fowler's position with a padded table for the patient to lean on.

questions.rationale: Relief from pericardial pain is often obtained by sitting up and leaning forward. Pain is increased by lying flat. Antiinflammatory medications may also be used to help control pain, but opioids are not usually indicated. The pain has a sharp, pleuritic quality that changes with respiration, and patients take shallow breaths.

questions.question: When obtaining a nursing history for a patient with myocarditis, what would the nurse question the patient about?

choices.text: Prior use of digoxin for treatment of cardiac problems
Recent symptoms of a viral illness, such as fever and malaise
A history of coronary artery disease (CAD) with or without an MI
A recent streptococcal infection requiring treatment with penicillin

questions.rationale: Viruses are the most common cause of myocarditis in the United States, and early manifestations of myocarditis are often those of systemic viral infections. Myocarditis may also be associated with autoimmune disorders as well as with other microorganisms, drugs, or toxins. The patient with myocarditis is predisposed to drug-related dysrhythmias and toxicity with digoxin, so it is used very cautiously, if at all, in treatment of the condition, but digoxin does not lead to myocarditis. A streptococcal infection is more likely to lead to rheumatic fever.

questions.question: What is the most important role of the nurse in preventing rheumatic fever?

choices.text: Teach patients with infective endocarditis to adhere to antibiotic prophylaxis.
Identify patients with valvular heart disease who are at risk for rheumatic fever.
Encourage the use of antibiotics for treatment of all infections involving a sore throat.
Promote the early diagnosis and immediate treatment of group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

questions.rationale: Adequate treatment of group A streptococcal pharyngitis can prevent initial attacks of rheumatic fever and the development of rheumatic heart disease. Because streptococcal infection accounts for only about 20% of acute pharyngitis, cultures should be done to identify the organism and direct antibiotic therapy. Viral infections should not be treated with antibiotics. Prophylactic therapy is indicated in those who have valvular heart disease or have had rheumatic heart disease.

questions.question: What manifestations strongly support a diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever?

choices.text: Carditis, polyarthritis, and erythema marginatum
Polyarthritis, chorea, and decreased antistreptolysin-O titer
Organic heart murmurs, fever, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Positive C-reactive protein, elevated white blood cells (WBCs), and subcutaneous nodules

questions.rationale: Two major criteria; or 1 major and 2 minor criteria plus laboratory evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection indicate rheumatic fever. Major criteria for the diagnosis of rheumatic fever include evidence of carditis, polyarthritis, erythema marginatum, Sydenham's chorea (often very late), and subcutaneous nodules. Minor criteria include increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and/or increased C-reactive protein (CRP), fever, arthralgia.

questions.question: When teaching the patient with acute rheumatic fever, identify the rationale for the use of each drug in the treatment plan.

options.text: To eliminate any residual group A β-hemolytic streptococci; prevent spread of infection; prevent recurrent infection
Antiinflammatory effect to control fever and arthritic and joint manifestations
Antiinflammatory effect to control fever and inflammation of severe carditis
Antiinflammatory effect to control fever and joint manifestations

questions.rationale: Antibiotics eliminate residual group A β-hemolytic streptococci and prevent spread and recurrent infection. Aspirin controls fever and arthritic/joint manifestations. Corticosteroids control fever and inflammation of severe carditis. NSAIDs control fever and joint manifestations.

questions.question: A patient with rheumatic heart disease with carditis asks the nurse how long activity will be restricted. What is the best answer by the nurse?

choices.text: "Full activity will be allowed as soon as acute symptoms have subsided."
"Bed rest will be continued until symptoms of heart failure are controlled."
"Nonstrenuous activities can be performed as soon as antibiotics are started."
"Bed rest must be maintained until antiinflammatory therapy has been discontinued."

questions.rationale: When carditis is present in the patient with rheumatic fever, ambulation is postponed until any symptoms of heart failure are controlled with treatment, and activity cannot be resumed until acute inflammation has subsided. In the patient without cardiac involvement, ambulation may be permitted as soon as acute symptoms have subsided, and normal activity can be resumed when antiinflammatory therapy is discontinued.

questions.question: What effect does valvular regurgitation have on a patient?

choices.text: It causes a pressure gradient difference across an open valve.
A pericardial friction rub is heard on the right sternal border of the chest.
It leads to decreased flow of blood and hypertrophy of the preceding chamber.
There is a backward flow of blood and volume overload in the preceding chamber.

questions.rationale: Valvular regurgitation causes a backward flow of blood and volume overload in the preceding chamber. Without treatment, eventually hypertrophy of that chamber occurs. Stenosis causes a pressure gradient difference and decreased blood flow and hypertrophy of the preceding chamber. A pericardial friction rub is not related to valvular regurgitation but would be heard at the lower left sternal border of the chest.

questions.question: A registered nurse (RN) is working with a licensed practical nurse/licensed vocational nurse (LPN/VN) in caring for a group of patients on a cardiac telemetry unit. Which nursing activity could be delegated to the LPN?

choices.text: Explain the reason for planning frequent periods of rest.
Evaluate the patient's understanding of his disease process.
Monitor BP, heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), and arterial oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry (SpO2) before, during, and after ambulation.
Teach the patient which activities to choose that will gradually increase endurance.

questions.rationale: Monitoring vital signs before and after ambulation is the collection of data. Instructions should be provided to the LPN about what changes in these vital signs should be reported to the RN. The other actions listed are RN responsibilities.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes mitral valve prolapse?

choices.text: Rapid onset prevents left chamber dilation
May be caused by pulmonary hypertension
Buckling of valve into left atrium during ventricular systole
Rapid development of pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock

questions.rationale: Mitral valve prolapse is the buckling of the valve leaflets into the left atrium during ventricular systole. The rapid onset that prevents left chamber dilation and the rapid development of pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock occur with acute mitral regurgitation. Pulmonary hypertension may contribute to tricuspid valve disease.

questions.question: Which cardiac valve disorder causes a sudden onset of cardiovascular collapse?

choices.text: Mitral valve stenosis
Tricuspid valve disease
Pulmonic valve stenosis
Acute aortic regurgitation

questions.rationale: Acute aortic regurgitation causes a sudden cardiovascular collapse. With mitral valve stenosis, dyspnea is a prominent symptom, and embolization may result from chronic atrial fibrillation. With tricuspid and pulmonic valve diseases, stenosis occurs more often than regurgitation. Tricuspid valve stenosis results in right atrial enlargement and elevated systemic venous pressures. Pulmonic valve stenosis results in right ventricular hypertension and hypertrophy.

questions.question: The patient is admitted with angina, syncope, and dyspnea on exertion. During the assessment, the nurse auscultates a systolic murmur with a prominent S4. What does the nurse consider as the cause?

choices.text: Mitral valve stenosis
Aortic valve stenosis
Acute mitral valve regurgitation
Chronic mitral valve regurgitation

questions.rationale: Aortic valve stenosis is identified with the triad of angina, syncope, and dyspnea on exertion, as well as the systolic murmur and prominent S4 heart sound. Mitral valve stenosis manifests as exertional dyspnea, hemoptysis, fatigue, atrial fibrillation, and a diastolic murmur. Acute mitral valve regurgitation has a new systolic murmur with pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock rapidly developing. Chronic mitral valve regurgitation is identified with weakness, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, palpitations, an S3 gallop, and holosystolic murmur.

questions.question: Which drugs would the nurse expect to be prescribed for patients with a mechanical valve replacement?

choices.text: Oral nitrates
Anticoagulants
Atrial antidysrhythmics
β-adrenergic blocking agents

questions.rationale: Patients with mechanical valves have an increased risk for thromboembolism and require long-term anticoagulation to prevent systemic or pulmonary embolization. Nitrates are contraindicated for the patient with aortic stenosis because an adequate preload is necessary to open the stiffened aortic valve. Antidysrhythmics are used only if dysrhythmias occur and β-adrenergic blocking drugs may be used to control the heart rate if needed.

questions.question: A patient with symptomatic mitral valve prolapse has atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias. In addition to monitoring for decreased cardiac output related to the dysrhythmias, what is an important nursing intervention related to the dysrhythmias?

choices.text: Monitor breathing pattern related to hypervolemia.
Encourage calling for assistance when getting out of bed.
Give sleeping pills to decrease paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
Teach the patient exercises to prevent recurrence of dysrhythmias.

questions.rationale: Dysrhythmias often cause palpitations, lightheadedness, and dizziness and the patient should be carefully attended to prevent falls. Hypervolemia and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) would be apparent in the patient with heart failure. Exercises will not prevent dysrhythmias.

questions.question: Which patients would the nurse expect to be scheduled for percutaneous transluminal balloon valvuloplasty?

choices.text: Any patient with aortic regurgitation
Older patients with aortic regurgitation
Older patients with stenosis of any valve
Young adult patients with mild mitral valve stenosis

questions.rationale: This procedure has been used for repair of mitral, tricuspid, and pulmonic stenosis and less often for aortic stenosis. It is usually used for older patients and for those patients who are poor surgical risks because it is relatively easy and has good results and few complications.

questions.question: A patient is scheduled for an open surgical valvuloplasty of the mitral valve. What information about this surgery would the nurse use to plan care?

choices.text: Cardiopulmonary bypass is not required with this procedure.
Valve repair is a palliative measure, while valve replacement is curative.
The operative mortality rate is lower in valve repair than in valve replacement.
Patients with valve repair do not need postoperative anticoagulation as do those who have valve replacement.

questions.rationale: Repair of mitral or tricuspid valves has a lower operative mortality rate than does replacement and is usually the surgical procedure of choice for these valvular diseases. Open repair is more precise than closed repair and requires cardiopulmonary bypass during surgery. All types of valve surgery are palliative, not curative, and patients require lifelong health care. Anticoagulation therapy is used for all valve surgery for at least some time postoperatively.

questions.question: In which patient would a mechanical prosthetic valve be preferred over a biologic valve for valve replacement?

choices.text: 41-year-old man with peptic ulcer disease
22-year-old woman who wants to have children
35-year-old man with a history of seasonal asthma
62-year-old woman with early Alzheimer's disease

questions.rationale: Mechanical prosthetic valves require long-term anticoagulation, and this is a factor in deciding about the type of valve to use for replacement. Patients who cannot take anticoagulant therapy, such as patients at risk for hemorrhage, women of childbearing age, patients who may not be compliant with anticoagulation therapy, and patients over age 65 years may be candidates for the less durable biologic valves.

questions.question: Which statement by a patient after mechanical valve replacement indicates to the nurse that further instruction is needed?

choices.text: "I may begin an exercise program to gradually increase my cardiac tolerance."
"I will always need to have my blood checked once a month for its clotting function."
"I will take prophylactic antibiotics before I have dental or invasive medical procedures."
"The biggest risk I have during invasive health procedures is bleeding because of my anticoagulants."

questions.rationale: The greatest risk to a patient who has an artificial valve is the development of endocarditis with invasive medical or dental procedures, not bleeding. Before any of these procedures, antibiotic prophylaxis is necessary to prevent infection. Planning of an exercise program and monitoring anticoagulant therapy will be done.

questions.question: A patient is admitted with symptoms of cardiomyopathy (CMP) following radiation therapy. Which type of CMP would the nurse suspect?

choices.text: Dilated
Restrictive
Takotsubo
Hypertrophic

questions.rationale: A secondary cause of restrictive CMP is radiation treatment to the thorax with stiffness of the ventricular wall occurring. Dilated CMP may have a genetic link, follow infectious myocarditis, or be related to an autoimmune process or excess alcohol ingestion. Takotsubo CMP is an acute stress-related syndrome that mimics acute coronary syndrome. It is most common in postmenopausal women. Hypertrophic CMP has a genetic link in about one-half of all cases and is often seen in young athletic individuals.

questions.question: Which statements accurately describe dilated CMP? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Characterized by ventricular stiffness
The least common type of CMP
The hyperdynamic systolic function creates a diastolic failure
Echocardiogram reveals cardiomegaly with thin ventricular walls
Often follows an infective myocarditis or exposure to toxins or drugs
Differs from chronic heart failure in that there is no ventricular hypertrophy

questions.rationale: Dilated CMP, the most common type of CMP, reveals cardiomegaly with thin ventricular walls on echocardiogram, as there is no ventricular hypertrophy, and may follow an infective myocarditis. In addition, stasis of blood in the ventricles may contribute to systemic embolization. Restrictive CMP is the least common type and is characterized by ventricular stiffness. Hypertrophic CMP is characterized by massive ventricular hypertrophy and rapid, forceful contraction of the left ventricle, impaired relaxation (diastole), and obstructed aortic valve outflow.

questions.question: What would the nurse include when planning care for the patient with hypertrophic CMP?

choices.text: Ventricular pacing
Administration of vasodilators
Teach the patient to avoid strenuous activity and dehydration
Surgery for cardiac transplantation will have to be done soon

questions.rationale: Nursing interventions for the patient with hypertrophic CMP are to improve ventricular filling by reducing ventricular contractility and relieving left ventricular outflow obstruction to relieve symptoms and prevent complications. Strenuous activity and dehydration will increase systemic vascular resistance and should be avoided. Atrioventricular pacing will allow the septum to move away from the left ventricular wall and reduce the degree of outflow obstruction. Vasodilators may decrease venous return and further increase obstruction of blood flow from the heart. The surgery that could be done involves cutting into the thickened septal wall and removing some of the ventricular muscle.

questions.question: When providing discharge teaching for any patient with CMP, what would the nurse teach the patient to do? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Eat a low-sodium diet.
Go to the gym every day.
Engage in stress reduction activities.
Abstain from alcohol and caffeine intake.
Avoid strenuous activity and allow for periods of rest.
Suggest that caregivers learn cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

questions.rationale: These topics can apply to any patient with CMP. Going to the gym could only be included within the exercise guidelines from the HCP and balanced with rest.

questions.question: When obtaining a health history from a 72-year-old man with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) of the lower extremities, which condition would the nurse consider is related?

choices.text: Venous thrombosis
Venous stasis ulcers
Pulmonary embolism
Coronary artery disease (CAD)

questions.rationale: Regardless of the location, atherosclerosis is responsible for PAD and is related to other cardiovascular disease and its risk factors, such as CAD and carotid artery disease. Venous thrombosis, venous stasis ulcers, and pulmonary embolism are diseases of the veins and are not related to atherosclerosis.

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient with chronic arterial disease has a brachial systolic blood pressure (SBP) of 132 mm Hg and an ankle SBP of 102 mm Hg. What is the ankle-brachial index (ABI)? (Round to 2 decimals.)
questions.rationale: ABI = ankle SBP / brachial SBP = 102 / 132 = 0.77.

questions.question: A patient has an ankle-brachial index of 0.77 (ankle SBP 102 / brachial SBP 132). What does this ABI indicate?

choices.text: Mild arterial disease
Moderate arterial disease
Severe arterial disease

questions.rationale: 102 / 132 = 0.77, which indicates mild arterial disease (see Table 41.3).

questions.question: Following teaching about medications for PAD, the nurse determines that additional instruction is needed when the patient states:

choices.text: "I can take 1 aspirin a day to prevent clotting in my legs."
"The lisinopril I use for my blood pressure may help me walk further without pain."
"I will need to have frequent blood tests to evaluate the effect of the pentoxifylline I will be taking."
"Cilostazol will help me increase my walking distance and speed and help prevent pain in my legs."

questions.rationale: Pentoxifylline allows blood cells to pass through small vessels, but there are no blood tests related to it. Warfarin (Coumadin), which needs international normalized ratio (INR) blood tests, is not recommended for prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD) events in patients with PAD. All the other statements are correct in relation to treatment of PAD.

questions.question: A patient with PAD has a clinical problem of ineffective tissue perfusion. What would be included in the teaching plan for this patient? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Apply cold compresses when the legs become swollen.
Wear protective footwear and avoid hot or cold extremes.
Walk at least 30 minutes per day, at least 3 times per week.
Use nicotine replacement therapy as a substitute for smoking.
Inspect lower extremities for pulses, skin, temperature, and any injury.

questions.rationale: Protecting feet and legs from injury is important. Walking exercise increases oxygen extraction in the legs and improves skeletal muscle metabolism. The patient with PAD should walk at least 30 minutes a day, at least 3 times per week. Exercise should be stopped when pain occurs and resumed when the pain subsides. The lower extremities should be assessed at regular intervals for changes. Cold compresses and nicotine in all forms causes vasoconstriction and should be avoided.

questions.question: When teaching the patient with PAD about modifying risk factors associated with the condition, what would the nurse emphasize?

choices.text: Amputation is the ultimate outcome if the patient does not alter lifestyle behaviors.
Modifications will reduce the risk of other atherosclerotic conditions, such as stroke.
Risk-reducing behaviors started after angioplasty can stop the progression of the disease.
Maintenance of normal body weight is the most important factor in controlling arterial disease.

questions.rationale: PAD occurs as a result of atherosclerosis and the risk factors are the same as for other diseases associated with atherosclerosis, such as CAD, cerebrovascular disease, and aneurysms. Major risk factors are tobacco use, hyperlipidemia, elevated C-reactive protein, diabetes, obesity, and uncontrolled hypertension. The risk for amputation is high in patients with severe occlusive disease, but this is not the best approach to encourage patients to make lifestyle modifications.

questions.question: During care of the patient following femoral bypass graft surgery, what assessment finding would the nurse immediately notify the health care provider (HCP) about?

choices.text: Fever and redness at the incision site
2+ edema of the extremity and pain at the incision site
A loss of palpable pulses and numbness and tingling of the feet
Increasing ankle-brachial indices and serous drainage from the incision

questions.rationale: Loss of palpable pulses, numbness and tingling of the extremity, extremity pallor, cyanosis, or cold are indications of occlusion of the bypass graft and need immediate medical attention. Pain, redness, and serous drainage at the incision site are expected postoperatively. Ankle brachial index measurements are not recommended because of increased risk for graft thrombosis, but this would decrease with occlusion.

questions.question: A patient has atrial fibrillation and develops an acute arterial occlusion at the iliac artery bifurcation. Name the 6 Ps of acute arterial occlusion (any order).
questions.rationale: The 6 Ps are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia. The HCP requires immediate notification to begin immediate intervention to prevent tissue necrosis and gangrene.

questions.question: Which conditions characterize critical limb ischemia? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Cold feet
Arterial leg ulcers
Venous leg ulcers
Gangrene of the leg
No palpable peripheral pulses
Rest pain lasting more than 2 weeks

questions.rationale: Arterial leg ulcers and/or gangrene of the leg caused by PAD and chronic ischemic rest pain lasting more than 2 weeks characterize critical limb ischemia. Optimal therapy is revascularization via bypass surgery.

questions.question: What are characteristics of vasospastic disease (Raynaud's phenomenon)? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Predominant in young females
May be associated with autoimmune disorders
Precipitated by exposure to cold, caffeine, and tobacco
Involves small cutaneous arteries of the fingers and toes
Inflammation of small and medium-sized arteries and veins
Episodes involve white, blue, and red color changes of fingertips

questions.rationale: Raynaud's phenomenon is predominant in young females and may be associated with autoimmune disorders (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, systemic lupus erythematosus). Incidents occur with cold, emotional upsets, and caffeine or tobacco use because of vasoconstrictive effects. Small cutaneous arteries are involved and cause color changes of the fingertips or toes. When conservative management is ineffective, it may be treated with nifedipine (Procardia).

questions.question: Which aneurysm is uniform in shape and a circumferential dilation of the artery?

choices.text: False aneurysm
Pseudoaneurysm
Saccular aneurysm
Fusiform aneurysm

questions.rationale: The fusiform aneurysm is circumferential and relatively uniform in shape. The false aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm is not an aneurysm but a disruption of all the arterial wall layers with bleeding that is contained by surrounding anatomic structures. Saccular aneurysms are the pouchlike bulge of an artery.

questions.question: A surgical repair is planned for a patient who has a 5.5-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). When assessing the patient, what would the nurse expect to find?

choices.text: Hoarseness and dysphagia
Severe back pain with flank ecchymosis
Presence of a bruit in the periumbilical area
Weakness in the lower extremities progressing to paraplegia

questions.rationale: Although most AAAs are asymptomatic, on physical examination a pulsatile mass in the periumbilical area slightly to the left of the midline may be detected and bruits may be audible with a stethoscope placed over the aneurysm. Hoarseness and dysphagia may occur with aneurysms of the ascending aorta and the aortic arch. Severe back pain with flank ecchymosis is usually present on rupture of an AAA and neurovascular loss in the lower extremities may occur from pressure of a thoracic aneurysm.

questions.question: A thoracic aortic aneurysm is identified when a patient has a routine chest x-ray. Which test would the nurse anticipate to determine the size and structure of the aneurysm?

choices.text: Angiography
Ultrasonography
Echocardiography
CT scan

questions.rationale: A CT scan is the most accurate test to determine the length and diameter of the aneurysm and whether a thrombus is present. The other tests may also be used, but the CT scan yields the most descriptive results.

questions.question: A patient with a small AAA is not a good surgical candidate. What would the nurse teach the patient is the best way to prevent expansion of the lesion?

choices.text: Avoid strenuous physical exertion.
Control hypertension with prescribed therapy.
Comply with prescribed anticoagulant therapy.
Maintain a low-calcium diet to prevent calcification of the vessel.

questions.rationale: Increased systolic BP (SBP) continually puts pressure on the diseased area of the artery, promoting its expansion. Small aneurysms can be treated by decreasing BP, modifying atherosclerosis risk factors, and monitoring the size of the aneurysm. Anticoagulants are used during surgical treatment of aneurysms, but physical activity is not known to increase their size. Calcium intake is not related to calcification in arteries.

questions.question: During preoperative preparation of the patient scheduled for an AAA, why would the nurse obtain a baseline patient assessment?

choices.text: All physiologic processes will be changed postoperatively.
The cause of the aneurysm is a systemic vascular disease.
Surgery will be canceled if any physiologic function is not normal.
BP and heart rate (HR) will be maintained well below baseline levels during the postoperative period.

questions.rationale: Because atherosclerosis is a systemic disease, the patient with an AAA is likely to have cardiac, pulmonary, cerebral, or lower extremity vascular problems that should be noted and monitored throughout the perioperative period. Postoperatively, the BP is balanced: high enough to keep adequate flow through the artery to prevent thrombosis but low enough to prevent bleeding at the surgical site.

questions.question: Which surgical therapy for an AAA is most likely to have the postoperative complication of renal injury?

choices.text: Open aneurysm repair (OAR) above the level of the renal arteries
Excising only the weakened area of the artery and suturing the artery closed
Bifurcated graft used in aneurysm repair when the AAA extends into the iliac arteries
Endovascular graft procedure with an aortic graft inside the aneurysm via the femoral artery

questions.rationale: With the aortic cross-clamping proximal and distal to the aneurysm, the open aneurysm repair (OAR) above the renal artery may cause kidney injury from lack of blood flow during the surgery. The saccular aneurysm may involve excising only the weakened area of the artery and suturing the artery closed, but this will not decrease renal blood flow. Renal blood flow will not be directly obstructed using the bifurcated graft or the minimally invasive endovascular aneurysm repair.

questions.question: What would the nurse include when teaching a patient preparing for AAA repair surgery?

choices.text: Prepare the bowel on the night before surgery with laxatives or an enema.
Use moisturizing soap to clean the skin three times the day before surgery.
Eat a high-protein and high-carbohydrate breakfast to help with healing postoperatively.
Take the prescribed oral antibiotic the morning of surgery before going to the operating room.

questions.rationale: Usually aortic surgery patients will have a bowel preparation, skin cleansing with an antimicrobial agent on the day before surgery, nothing by mouth after midnight on the day of the surgery, and IV antibiotics immediately before the incision is made. Patients with a history of CVD will receive a β-adrenergic blocker preoperatively to reduce morbidity and mortality. Each surgeon's protocol may be different.

questions.question: During the acute postoperative period following repair of an AAA, which patient goal would the nurse ensure is achieved?

choices.text: Hypothermia is maintained to decrease oxygen need.
IV fluids are given to maintain urine output of 100 mL/hr.
BP and all peripheral pulses are assessed at least every hour.
BP is kept lower than baseline to prevent leaking at the incision line.

questions.rationale: The BP and peripheral pulses are evaluated every hour in the acute postoperative period to ensure that BP is adequate to maintain graft patency and that extremities are being perfused. BP is kept within normal range. If BP is too low, thrombosis of the graft may occur; if it is too high, it may cause leaking or rupture at the suture line. Hypothermia is induced during surgery, but the patient is rewarmed as soon as surgery is over. Fluid replacement to maintain urine output at 100 mL/hr would increase the BP too much and only 30 mL/hr of urine is needed to show adequate renal perfusion.

questions.question: Following an ascending aortic aneurysm repair, what assessment finding would the nurse immediately report to the HCP?

choices.text: Shallow respirations and poor coughing
Decreased drainage from the chest tubes
A change in level of consciousness and inability to speak
Lower extremity pulses that are decreased from the preoperative baseline

questions.rationale: During repair of an ascending aortic aneurysm, the blood supply to the carotid arteries may be interrupted, leading to neurologic complications manifested by a decreased level of consciousness (LOC) and altered pupil responses to light as well as changes in facial symmetry, speech, upper extremity movement, and hand grasp quality. The thorax is opened for ascending aortic surgery, and shallow breathing, poor cough, and decreasing chest drainage are expected. Lower limb pulses may normally be decreased or absent for a short time following surgery.

questions.question: Which assessment finding would alert the nurse that the patient may have graft thrombosis after an AAA repair?

choices.text: Dysrhythmias or chest pain
Absent bowel sounds, abdominal distention, or diarrhea
Increased temperature and increased white blood cell count
Decreased pulses and cool, painful extremities below the level of repair

questions.rationale: Decreased or absent pulses in conjunction with cool, painful extremities below the level of repair indicate graft thrombosis. Dysrhythmias or chest pain indicates myocardial ischemia. Absent bowel sounds, abdominal distention, diarrhea, or bloody stools indicate bowel infarction. Increased temperature and white blood cells (WBCs), surgical site inflammation, or drainage indicates graft infection.

questions.question: A patient who is status-post repair of an AAA has been receiving IV fluids at 125 mL/hr continuously for the last 12 hours. Urine output for the last 4 hours has been 60 mL, 42 mL, 28 mL, and 20 mL, respectively. What action would the nurse take?

choices.text: Monitor for a couple more hours.
Contact the HCP and report the decrease in urine output.
Send blood for electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine.
Decrease the rate of infusion to prevent blood leakage at the suture line.

questions.rationale: The decreasing urine output is evidence that either the patient needs volume replacement or there is reduced renal blood flow. The HCP will want to be notified as soon as possible of this change in condition and will request results of daily BUN and serum creatinine levels. The other options are incorrect.

questions.question: Following discharge teaching with a male patient with an AAA repair, the nurse determines that further instruction is needed when the patient makes which statement?

choices.text: "I should avoid heavy lifting for 6 weeks."
"I may have some sexual dysfunction because of the surgery."
"I should maintain a low-fat and low-cholesterol diet to help keep the new graft open."
"I will take the pulses in my legs and let the doctor know if they get too fast or too slow."

questions.rationale: Patients are taught to palpate peripheral pulses to identify changes in their quality or strength, but the rate is not a significant factor in peripheral perfusion. The color and temperature of the extremities are important for patients to observe. The remaining statements are true.

questions.question: During the assessment of the patient with a type B aortic dissection, what would the nurse expect the patient to manifest?

choices.text: Altered level of consciousness (LOC) with dizziness and weak carotid pulses
A cardiac murmur characteristic of aortic valve insufficiency
Severe "ripping" back or abdominal pain with decreased urine output
Severe hypertension and orthopnea and dyspnea of pulmonary edema

questions.rationale: A Type B aortic dissection involves the distal descending aorta and is usually characterized by a sudden, severe, tearing pain in the back. As it progresses down the aorta, the kidneys, abdominal organs, and lower extremities may begin to show evidence of ischemia. Type A aortic dissections of the ascending aorta and aortic arch may affect the heart and circulation to the head, with the development of cerebral ischemia, murmurs, ventricular failure, and pulmonary edema.

questions.question: A patient with a type A dissection of the arch of the aorta has a decreased LOC and weak carotid pulses. What would the nurse anticipate that initial treatment of the patient will include?

choices.text: Immediate surgery to replace the torn area with a graft
Administration of anticoagulants to prevent embolization
Administration of packed red blood cells (RBCs) to replace blood loss
Giving antihypertensives to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 70 to 80 mm Hg

questions.rationale: Immediate surgery is indicated when complications (such as occlusion of the carotid arteries) occur. Otherwise, initial treatment for aortic dissection involves a period of lowering the BP and myocardial contractility to diminish the pulsatile forces in the aorta. Anticoagulants would prolong and intensify the bleeding. Blood is given only if the dissection ruptures.

questions.question: What indicates to the nurse that treatment for the patient with an uncomplicated aortic dissection is successful?

choices.text: Pain is relieved.
Surgical repair is completed.
BP is increased to normal range.
Renal output is maintained at 30 mL/hr.

questions.rationale: Relief of pain is a sign that the dissection has stabilized, and it may be treated conservatively for an extended time with drugs that lower the BP and decrease myocardial contractility. Surgery is usually indicated for Type A aortic dissection or if complications occur.

questions.question: What are characteristics of PAD? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Pruritus
Thickened, brittle nails
Dull ache in calf or thigh
Decreased peripheral pulses
Pallor on elevation of the legs
Ulcers over bony prominences on toes and feet

questions.rationale: PAD is manifested as thick, brittle nails; decreased peripheral pulses; pallor when the legs are elevated; ulcers over bony prominences on the toes and feet; and paresthesia. The other options are characteristic of venous disease and paresthesia could occur with venous thromboembolism (VTE).

questions.question: The patient is diagnosed with a superficial vein thrombosis (SVT). Which characteristic would the nurse know about SVT?

choices.text: Embolization to lungs may result in death.
Clot may extend to deeper veins if untreated.
Vein is tender to pressure and there is edema.
Typically found in the iliac, inferior, or superior vena cava.

questions.rationale: If left untreated, a superficial vein thrombosis (SVT) may extend to deeper veins and VTE may occur. VTE may embolize to the lungs and have tenderness to pressure and edema. SVTs usually occur in superficial leg veins and have tenderness, itchiness, redness, warmth, pain, inflammation, and induration along the course of the superficial vein.

questions.question: The nurse receives report about a 68-year-old female being admitted after a lengthy hip replacement surgery. Her history includes smoking and taking hormone therapy. What risk factors increase her risk for developing venous thromboembolism (VTE) related to Virchow's triad? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Smoking
IV therapy
Dehydration
Estrogen therapy
Orthopedic surgery
Prolonged immobilization

questions.rationale: This patient is a smoker and on hormone therapy, both of which increase blood hypercoagulability. She will have an IV, and her fractured hip can cause VTE by damaging the venous endothelium. She is an older patient who has had an orthopedic surgery and may have experienced prolonged immobility postinjury and through her "lengthy hip replacement surgery," which contributes to venous stasis. These are representative of Virchow's triad in this patient. The other options are also related to Virchow's triad but not present in this patient via the transfer report.

questions.question: The patient comes to the HCP office with pain, edema, and warm skin on her lower left leg. What test would the nurse expect to be ordered first?

choices.text: Duplex ultrasound
Complete blood count (CBC)
Magnetic resonance angiography
Computed venography (phlebogram)

questions.rationale: With manifestations of a VTE, the Duplex ultrasound is most widely used to diagnose VTE by identifying where a thrombus is found and its extent. D-dimer may also be drawn to determine if a VTE exists.

questions.question: What care could the registered nurse (RN) delegate to the assistive personnel (AP) for a patient with VTE?

choices.text: Assess the patient's use of herbs.
Measure the patient for elastic compression stockings.
Remind the patient to flex and extend the legs and feet every 2 hours.
Teach the patient to call emergency response system with signs of pulmonary embolus.

questions.rationale: The RN could delegate to the AP the task to remind the patient to flex and extend the legs and feet every 2 hours while in bed. Measuring for elastic compression stockings may be delegated to the LPN. The RN must assess and teach the patient.

questions.question: To help prevent embolization of a thrombus in a patient with acute VTE and severe edema and limb pain, what would the nurse teach the patient to do first?

choices.text: Dangle on the edge of the bed q2-3hr.
Ambulate around the bed 3 to 4 times a day.
Keep the affected leg elevated above the level of the heart.
Maintain bed rest until edema is relieved and anticoagulation is established.

questions.rationale: With acute VTE, prevention of emboli formation, decreased edema and pain can be achieved initially by bed rest and limiting movement of the involved extremity. Ambulation will be the next priority. Dangling the legs promotes venous stasis and further clot formation. Elevating the affected limb will promote venous return, but it does not prevent embolization.

questions.question: Which indirect thrombin inhibitor is only given subcutaneously and does not need routine coagulation tests?

choices.text: Warfarin (Coumadin)
Unfractionated heparin
Hirudin derivatives (bivalirudin [Angiomax])
Low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin [Lovenox])

questions.rationale: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) (enoxaparin [Lovenox]) is only given subcutaneously and does not need routine coagulation testing. Unfractionated heparin is the only other indirect thrombin inhibitor option. It can be given subcutaneously or IV and therapeutic effects must be monitored with coagulation testing.

questions.question: Which characteristics describe the anticoagulant warfarin (Coumadin)? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Vitamin K is the antidote
Protamine sulfate is the antidote
May be given orally or subcutaneously
May be given intravenously or subcutaneously
Monitor dosage using international normalized ratio (INR)
Monitor dosage using activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)

questions.rationale: Warfarin (Coumadin) is a vitamin K antagonist, so vitamin K is the antidote. It is monitored with the INR. It is only given orally. Protamine sulfate is the antidote for unfractionated heparin (UH) and LMWH. UH can be given subcutaneously or IV. It is monitored with aPTT. Hirudin derivatives are given IV or subcutaneously, do not have an antidote, and are monitored with aPTT. Argatroban, a synthetic thrombin inhibitor, is given only IV and is monitored with aPTT. Factor Xa inhibitor, fondaparinux (Arixtra), is given subcutaneously and does not need routine coagulation testing. Rivaroxaban (Xarelto), another factor Xa inhibitor, is given orally.

questions.question: The patient with VTE is receiving therapy with heparin and asks the nurse whether the drug will dissolve the clot in her leg. What is the best response by the nurse?

choices.text: "This drug will break up and dissolve the clot so that circulation in the vein can be restored."
"The purpose of the heparin is to prevent growth of the clot or formation of new clots where the circulation is slowed."
"Heparin won't dissolve the clot, but it will inhibit the inflammation around the clot and delay the development of new clots."
"The heparin will dilate the vein, preventing turbulence of blood flow around the clot that may cause it to break off and travel to the lungs."

questions.rationale: Anticoagulant therapy with heparin or warfarin (Coumadin) does not dissolve clots but prevents propagation of the clot, development of new thrombi, and embolization. Clot lysis occurs naturally through the body's intrinsic fibrinolytic system or by the administration of thrombolytic agents.

questions.question: A patient with VTE being discharged on long-term warfarin (Coumadin) therapy is taught about prevention and continuing treatment of VTE. The nurse determines that discharge teaching has been effective when the patient makes which statement?

choices.text: "I should expect that Coumadin will cause my stools to be somewhat black."
"I should avoid all dark green and leafy vegetables while I am taking Coumadin."
"Massaging my legs several times a day will help increase my venous circulation."
"Swimming is a good activity to include in my exercise program to increase my circulation."

questions.rationale: Exercise programs for patients recovering from VTE should emphasize swimming, which is particularly beneficial because of the gentle, even pressure of the water. Coumadin will not blacken stools. If this occurs, it could be a sign of gastrointestinal bleeding. Dark green and leafy vegetables have high amounts of vitamin K and should not be increased during Coumadin therapy, but they do not need to be restricted. The legs must not be massaged because of the risk for dislodging any clots that may be present.

questions.question: What would the nurse teach the patient with any venous disorder is the best way to prevent venous stasis and increase venous return?

choices.text: Take short walks.
Sit with the legs elevated.
Frequently rotate the ankles.
Always wear elastic compression stockings.

questions.rationale: During walking, the muscles of the legs continuously knead the veins, promoting movement of venous blood toward the heart. Walking is the best measure to prevent venous stasis and will be increased gradually. Elevating the legs will decrease edema. The other methods will help venous return, but they do not provide the benefit that ambulation does.

questions.question: Number the processes from 1 (the first) to 9 (the last) that occur as venous stasis leads to varicose veins and venous leg ulcers.

items.prompt: Blood supply to local tissues decreases

questions.rationale: Order: 1. venous pressure increases; 2. veins dilate; 3. venous valves become incompetent; 4. venous blood flow backs up; 5. additional venous distention occurs; 6. capillary pressure increases; 7. edema forms; 8. blood supply to local tissues decreases; 9. ulceration occurs.

questions.question: What is the most important measure in the treatment of venous leg ulcers?

choices.text: Elevation of the affected leg
Application of topical antibiotics
Graduated compression stockings
Application of moist to dry dressings

questions.rationale: Although leg elevation, moist dressings, and systemic antibiotics are useful in treatment of venous stasis ulcers, the most important factor is compression, which minimizes venous stasis, venous hypertension, and edema and prevents recurrence. Compression may be applied with various methods including stockings, elastic bandages or wraps, or a Velcro wrap, among others.
